title: Leadership Chiarelli, Andrea Trapped In Your Business
author: Chiarelli, Andrea
summary: Andrea Chiarelli reviews Peter Bergeron's 'The Trapped Operator,' which argues that the named problem a business presents is almost never the real problem -- it is a signal from an underlying architectural condition. The diagnostic shift is from 'what caused this?' to 'which underlying system is failing to contain the pressure producing this?' -- two questions that generate entirely different conversations. Bergeron replaces the traditional business lifecycle with three recurring operational states (survival, scale, stability) that a business can cycle through non-linearly, meaning the fixes that worked in one state stop holding when the business shifts load. A key theme is the vocabulary problem: business owners often feel the weight of dysfunction but cannot describe it clearly, and Bergeron's framework of 12 recurring issues gives them language that produces recognition. The core test: could the organization survive a sustained absence of its founder?
points: * The named problem is almost always a signal, not the root: treating each problem as a discrete event produces the same problems returning in slightly different disguises, because the underlying architectural condition generating the signal was never addressed. * The diagnostic reframe from 'what caused this?' to 'which underlying system is failing to contain the pressure producing this?' looks like a semantic shift but generates entirely different conversations and interventions. * Operational states are non-linear: a mature company hit by a new competitor can re-enter survival conditions within twelve months -- the fixes that held at one stage stop holding when the load changes. * Giving people vocabulary they recognize themselves in is a diagnostic act: owners who see their situation in Bergeron's 12 recurring issues often experience relief at discovering it is a documented condition, not a personal failing. * The ownership test -- could the organization survive a sustained absence of its founder? -- is almost impossible for founders to answer honestly because their own indispensability is the water they swim in.
quotes: A vendor calls about an overdue invoice. A senior employee gives notice. Each event arrives with its own face and its own apparent cause, and it is easy to end up addressing each one directly.
The diagnostic alternative he advocates is to stop asking 'What caused this?' and start asking 'Which underlying system is failing to contain the pressure that is producing this?'
A business doesn't move through these in sequence and exit them in a linear way. These are parts of a cycle, and a business can go back and forth across its history.

When Bergeron names 12 recurring issues -- inadequate capitalisation, client overdependence, ineffective marketing, ineffective management, and more -- he reports that business owners find their own situation in the list within minutes.
The methodological warning here is that the line between giving someone the vocabulary they need and putting words in their mouth is not always obvious. Telling the two apart is most of the craft.
A business with a thin marketing function can run for years if its customer service and word-of-mouth are strong enough to compensate.
Founders struggle to answer this honestly because their own indispensability is the water they swim in.
